Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
go along with whatever others want to feel safe

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette:
Rajan was forty-one years old, a park ranger in a sprawling national forest on the West Coast, a job he had loved for its solitude and its order, the clear trails and the predictable rhythms of the seasons. He lived with his partner in a small house at the edge of the woods, and for years his life had felt steady, even peaceful. That had ended three years ago, during a six-week period of captivity that he still could not fully speak about, a time when he had been held in a basement by men who wore uniforms and who talked endlessly about military tactics, about chains of command, about what they called discipline. He had been taken because of a mistaken identity, a bureaucratic error that no one would later acknowledge, and for forty-two days he had been kept in a room with no windows, fed irregularly, beaten when he asked questions, and made to feel that his entire existence had been reduced to the whim of people who saw him as nothing.

The memory of it did not come back as a story. It came back as snapshots, a series of still images that would appear without warning: the crack in the ceiling above the cot, the smell of diesel fuel on the guard's jacket, the exact weight of the metal chair against his spine. When these images arrived, they were not accompanied by emotion. Sometimes he could recall the whole sequence and feel absolutely nothing, as if he were watching a film about a stranger, a man who had been too weak or too foolish to avoid capture. And then, at other times, the memory would arrive as pure physical sensation: a sharp, grinding pain in his lower back, exactly where he had been forced to sit for hours without moving, or a burning ache in his wrists, where the zip ties had cut into his skin. He could not predict which version would surface, and he had come to dread both.

The men who had held him had been obsessed with rank and procedure. Now, any person in uniform-a police officer, a security guard, even a postal carrier-made Rajan's chest tighten and his vision narrow. He could not help but scan their hands, their belts, their faces for signs of the cold, procedural cruelty he had learned to expect. He had also developed a deep, unshakable certainty that he was never safe, even when his partner or his doctor told him otherwise. He would be standing in the middle of a quiet trail, alone, and a sudden movement in the underbrush-a deer, a hiker stepping out from behind a tree-would make him flinch so violently that he would drop whatever he was holding, his heart slamming against his ribs as if the basement door had just opened.

He had changed his life in ways that were invisible to most people but that felt essential to his survival. He had stopped eating regular meals, instead controlling every calorie with a rigid precision that gave him the only sense of agency he still possessed. He had also begun to say yes to everything his partner suggested, agreeing to any plan, any movie, any restaurant, because disagreeing felt dangerous, felt like it might provoke the kind of confrontation that had once cost him everything. In the privacy of his own mind, however, he spent hours constructing elaborate revenge fantasies, imagining what he would do if he ever found the men again, scenarios that left him shaking and ashamed but that he could not stop replaying.

The worst of it was the feeling of permanent humiliation, a stain he could not scrub away. He believed, with a certainty that felt like fact, that someone else-someone stronger, smarter, more resourceful-would never have been taken in the first place. Someone else would have seen it coming. Someone else would have fought back. He had not fought back. He had complied, and that compliance felt like a betrayal of himself that he could never undo. He felt isolated from everyone, even from his partner, because he was certain that no one could understand what it meant to have been so completely erased.

What finally brought him to seek help was not the flashbacks or the startle responses, though those had worsened. It was the moment he found himself standing in the middle of a trail, staring at a family of hikers who had asked him a simple question about the route, and realizing he could not form words. His throat had closed, his hands had gone numb, and he had simply walked away, leaving them confused and worried. He had driven home, called his partner, and said, for the first time, that he needed to talk to someone. He was afraid of what that might mean-afraid that speaking about it would make it more real, afraid that he would be judged, afraid that the humiliation would deepen. But he was also, quietly, hoping that somewhere inside the telling, he might find a way to stop being the person who had been taken.
